brief.head: Friends in tiers
brief.text: Ajay Shah, cit­ing Dunbar’s num­ber, makes de­lib­er­ate ef­fort for his clos­est few. Friendships have their mo­ments, he said: “no man walks in the same friend­ship twice.” {017-C01}

brief.head: Dream, don’t count
brief.text: Technology and GDP will prob­a­bly im­prove, Ajay Shah said, but a society’s progress is far more com­plex. Many coun­tries have gone ter­ri­bly wrong, so it is not guar­an­teed. {017-C03}

brief.head: Unlikely is inevitable
brief.text: Lose five poker hands in a row as an 80 per cent favourite and you may cry foul. Given enough hands, Amit Varma said, such runs are bound to hap­pen. {017-R12}

brief.head: Patriots at the board
brief.text: Amit Varma’s pa­tri­ots are the top Russian chess play­ers who wrote against Putin after the in­va­sion. Many can no longer enter Russia and now play for other coun­tries. {017-S07}

brief.head: Beyond any gamer
brief.text: For an AI re­searcher in China the ex­port con­trols are a catas­tro­phe, Ajay Shah said. But the chips barred are “way be­yond any­thing a gamer will want”. {#gamer}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on globalisation’s rise, fall and return
lead.head: Still global, now with a bouncer

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 17

body: Many peo­ple have writ­ten globalisation’s obit­u­ary. Ajay Shah, who coined a term for what is hap­pen­ing in­stead, thinks they are wrong. “It’s not true that glob­al­iza­tion is dead,” he said, “but that the perime­ter has shrunk.” {017-C11}

Talking to Amit Varma, Shah told the story in waves: a first glob­al­i­sa­tion of near-total free­dom, a long dark chap­ter ruled by na­tion states, a sec­ond that wel­comed ev­ery­one, and now a third that asks its mem­bers to be­have.
## Five flows, two forces

Shah began by tak­ing the tired word apart. Globalisation, he said, is about five things cross­ing bor­ders through vol­un­tary trans­ac­tions: ideas, peo­ple, goods, ser­vices and cap­i­tal. {017-C04}

Two forces push it up and down. One is the state, which bans books, is­sues pass­ports, levies cus­toms du­ties and im­poses cap­i­tal con­trols. The other is tech­nol­ogy. “It’s about the death of dis­tance,” Shah said.
Varma put the philo­soph­i­cal ques­tion plainly. If friends in Mozambique and Pune both want to sell you ball bear­ings in Mumbai, he asked, why should it be harder for the one in Mozambique?
## Paradise lost, and re­gained

Steamships, the Suez Canal and the tele­graph set off the first glob­al­i­sa­tion. States stayed out of the way. People trav­elled with­out pass­ports, and cap­i­tal raised in London flowed down­hill to the United States, Argentina and India, where re­turns were higher.

Nationalism de­stroyed it. The First World War brought pass­ports and block­ades, Hitler im­posed the world’s first cap­i­tal con­trols, and the post-war order de­signed by John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White traded free cap­i­tal for fixed ex­change rates.
The world’s trade-to-GDP ratio, Shah said, only got back to its 1913 level in 1982. “We lost free­dom from 1913 to 1982, or maybe even a bit be­yond.” {017-C06}
The sec­ond glob­al­i­sa­tion that fol­lowed brought con­tainer ships, wide-body air­craft, com­put­ers and tele­com. India’s soft­ware and ser­vices boom, Shah said, came from plug­ging into it.
## Rules of the club
Then came eco­nomic state­craft: chips that may not be sold to China, Dutch ma­chines that may not be shipped there, Russian cen­tral bank re­serves grabbed after the in­va­sion of Ukraine.

The sec­ond glob­al­i­sa­tion had let ev­ery­one in with­out con­di­tions. “We felt con­fi­dent that as you be­come rich, you will in­evitably stop beat­ing your wife,” Shah said. Instead China grew more au­thor­i­tar­ian, and Gorbachev’s Russia be­came Putin’s.

Now, he ar­gued, the ad­vanced economies, which in­clude Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, make good be­hav­iour a con­di­tion of entry, start­ing with not in­vad­ing your neigh­bour. About 85 per cent of world GDP is in­side the club, and there glob­al­i­sa­tion is deep­en­ing. {#club85}
Shah is not fussed. India, he said, is a sta­tus quo power that has no wish to con­quer Bangladesh. His ad­vice, bor­rowed from Deng Xiaoping: “bide your time.”
Varma was less com­fort­able. Those shut out, he said, are not rogue na­tions but “un­for­tu­nate peo­ple who hap­pen to be in coun­tries which have rogue regimes.”
On one thing the two agreed. Trade deficits, as Tim Harford’s babysit­ter shows, are no prob­lem at all: in­di­vid­u­als and firms trade, not coun­tries. {017-C13}
The episode began with friend­ship and Dunbar’s num­ber. It ended with Varma weep­ing in the rain over a pod­cast, and Shah lost in a book in an Irani cafe until 9 pm.

second.label: Randomness
second.head: Too random to be random
second.deck: Apple fixed its shuffle by breaking it, Amit Varma told Ajay Shah
body: When the iPod was first in­tro­duced, its shuf­fle played songs truly at ran­dom. Some lis­ten­ers com­plained: they had got six Bruce Springsteen songs in a row, and that could not be ran­dom.

“Given a long enough num­ber of it­er­a­tions,” Amit Varma said, “any un­likely thing will hap­pen.” {017-C16} Apple’s an­swer was an al­go­rithm that broke up such streaks, so the shuf­fle would ap­pear ran­dom with­out being ran­dom. {017-S03}

Ajay Shah of­fered the statistician’s view. The runs test checks ran­dom­ness by count­ing how often streaks of dif­fer­ent lengths occur. {#runstest} Fed data from the orig­i­nal iPod, he said, it would have de­liv­ered an ob­jec­tive ver­dict: “Apple, you are lying.”

quote.text: So how Apple dealt with this com­plaint was by in­tro­duc­ing an al­go­rithm which made it non-random

third.head: Soaked in a war story

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Dan Carlin’s war letters

body: Amit Varma started Dan Carlin’s World War One se­ries, *Blueprint for Armageddon*, on a run. {017-R23} When his one-hour work­out ended he could not go back up to his apart­ment, and stood below, still lis­ten­ing.

On an­other run it began to rain, and he stayed out. That day Carlin read the let­ters a group of sol­diers wrote to their wives and girl­friends the night be­fore a bat­tle in which they all died. {017-S05}
“And I was weep­ing in the rain,” Varma said. The se­ries has no script and no sound ef­fects: just one man talk­ing, “prac­ti­cally think­ing aloud”.
It taught him that a story needs noth­ing but a voice. Storytelling was humanity’s first en­ter­tain­ment, he said. “Audio is the most pow­er­ful medium in the world.” {017-C18}

box.title: A term of Ajay Shah’s own
box.text: Ajay Shah set out the idea in his ar­ti­cle *Dawn of the third globalisation?*: a world still glob­al­is­ing, but in­side a club with rules. The first and sec­ond glob­al­i­sa­tions are in the lit­er­a­ture, Amit Varma noted; the third is a term Shah coined. {#coined}

sections.label: The moral circle
sections.head: Who counts as one of us
sections.caption: the expanding circle
body: Before ships and tele­graphs could join the world, Amit Varma ar­gued, there was a glob­al­i­sa­tion of the mind. He took the idea from W.E.H. Lecky’s *History of European Morals*: the ex­pand­ing cir­cle. {017-R02}

Humans, Lecky said, begin by ex­tend­ing moral con­sid­er­a­tion to a small cir­cle, the fam­ily. Over his­tory it widens to friends, the tribe, the na­tion and be­yond. Everyone out­side it, Varma said, “might as well be an­i­mals”.
That ex­plains hor­rors such as slav­ery, he said: the cir­cle had not yet grown be­yond people’s own kind or skin colour. At one point it may not even have in­cluded women.
## Next, the an­i­mals

Peter Singer ar­gues that the cir­cle should reach an­i­mals. Varma ex­pects it will: just as Jefferson kept slaves and thought it morally fine, peo­ple two hun­dred years from now may look back on us and say “oh they ate an­i­mals.” {017-J13}

But cir­cles can also con­tract. With so much na­tion­al­ism and so much vir­u­lence about iden­tity, he said, “our cir­cles are shrink­ing and not ex­pand­ing, and that wor­ries me greatly.” {017-C02}

~ Ajay Shah, for his part, mar­velled that Mahavir and Jainism emerged in a prim­i­tive so­ci­ety short of pro­tein, which was no golden age. There, he said, some peo­ple “de­vel­oped very ad­vanced con­cepts and philoso­phies”.

quote.text: So it’s a very iffy thing, it’s some­thing to as­pire for. We should dream of it, but we should not count on it.

sections.label: Defining terms
sections.head: Five things that cross borders
sections.caption: what globalisation means
body: “By the time a word grad­u­ates into the air­port books,” Ajay Shah said, “it surely stops mak­ing much sense.” {017-J09} So he took glob­al­i­sa­tion apart.
Globalisation, he said, is the ex­tent to which five flows, aris­ing from vol­un­tary trans­ac­tions, are not shaped by a na­tional bor­der: ideas, peo­ple, goods, ser­vices and cap­i­tal.

States in­ter­fere with each. They ban books and ideas to push a con­ve­nient nar­ra­tive. They give every in­di­vid­ual a num­ber and put up a check post at the bor­der, a game Shah said began at the time of the First World War. They charge cus­toms du­ties on ball bear­ings from Mozambique.
## The small chicken

And they con­trol cap­i­tal in­tri­cately. In India, Shah said, poul­try farms and nan­otech­nol­ogy firms may bor­row abroad but oth­ers can­not. Amit Varma spot­ted the op­por­tu­nity: “If you’re a re­ally small chicken, you have the best of both worlds, poul­try farms and nano chicken.” {017-J01}
Against the state stands tech­nol­ogy. Container ships and air freight made it pos­si­ble to move ball bear­ings from Mozambique to India, and tele­com made ser­vices ex­portable.
~ The state it­self, Shah re­minded lis­ten­ers, is sim­ply “the com­mu­nity that achieves and main­tains a mo­nop­oly of phys­i­cal vi­o­lence in a given ter­ri­tory”. {#state}

quote.text: the term glob­al­iza­tion refers to the ex­tent to which these five things are not being shaped by a na­tional bor­der.

sections.label: Wave one
sections.head: Capital rolls downhill
sections.caption: the first globalisation
body: Steamships, the Suez Canal and the tele­graph set off the first glob­al­i­sa­tion, Ajay Shah said, as mes­sages, money and cot­ton began mov­ing be­tween the United States, the UK and India. {017-C05}
People trav­elled with­out pass­ports or visas, and a lawyer could go and prac­tise in London. The only con­straints were those of tech­nol­ogy.

An im­por­tant fea­ture, Shah said, was cap­i­tal mov­ing down­hill. London had so much cap­i­tal that one more fac­tory there earned lit­tle, while re­turns in the United States, Argentina and India were high. Projects ev­ery­where raised money in London and in­vested it where it earned more.
## The long dark chap­ter

“All this went to hell,” Shah said, with the First World War and the Russian Revolution. Passports ar­rived, Britain block­aded Germany, and German sub­marines fired on cargo ships. Hitler, want­ing to go after the Jews, brought in the world’s first cap­i­tal con­trols. {017-J12}

After 1945, John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White de­signed GATT, the World Bank and the IMF around fixed ex­change rates. Keynes knew in­tu­itively, Shah said, that you can­not man­age the ex­change rate and have an open cap­i­tal ac­count. {#keynes} So cap­i­tal con­trols stayed.
~ Amit Varma added that Keynes once wanted Chintaman Deshmukh as the IMF’s first man­ag­ing di­rec­tor, until the Americans ob­jected: “What Indian fel­low, what are you talk­ing about?” {017-J11}

quote.text: It’s im­por­tant to re­mem­ber that in the first glob­al­iza­tion, na­tion states were not in the game.

sections.label: Wave two
sections.head: When the state stepped aside
sections.caption: the second globalisation
body: From 1982, Ajay Shah said, the free­doms lost since the First World War began to re­turn. Container ships and wide-body air­craft cut trans­port costs, com­put­ers and tele­com made ser­vices trad­able, fixed ex­change rates gave way to float­ing ones, and cap­i­tal con­trols came off.

Within the European Union, visa-free travel let peo­ple take a bus across na­tional bor­ders. India, Shah said, was “a gi­gan­tic ben­e­fi­ciary”: its soft­ware and ser­vices rev­o­lu­tion came from plug­ging in.
## Better at both

Why does trade help? David Ricardo showed, Shah said, that it raises wel­fare even when one side is bet­ter at ev­ery­thing. What mat­ters is a dif­fer­ence in the ratio of how much bet­ter each side is at two things. {017-C08}
Amit Varma of­fered his own ver­sion: “I am a bet­ter pod­caster than you. I am also a bet­ter econ­o­mist than you.” Yet he does the pod­cast­ing and leaves the eco­nom­ics to Shah. {017-J02}

Shah’s test from pub­lic eco­nom­ics: in­ter­ven­tion is jus­ti­fied only by a mar­ket fail­ure, such as asym­met­ric in­for­ma­tion, an ex­ter­nal­ity or a pub­lic good. Buying ball bear­ings from Mozambique in­volves none of these. Without one, he said, in­ter­ven­tion harms wel­fare and GDP. {017-C09}
~ Varma added that a tar­iff re­dis­tributes from poor con­sumers at large to rich in­ter­est groups, and that vol­un­tary trade is con­sent, a pos­i­tive-sum game that state co­er­cion spoils.

quote.text: when the state in­ter­venes in the ab­sence of a mar­ket fail­ure it has an ad­verse im­pact on wel­fare.

sections.label: Wave three
sections.head: Don’t invade your neighbour
sections.caption: economic statecraft
body: In re­cent years, Ajay Shah said, things once unimag­in­able have begun to hap­pen, under a field called eco­nomic state­craft: using state power to in­ter­fere with the work­ing of the econ­omy. {#statecraft}

The United States blocked Chinese pur­chases of American busi­nesses and Dubai Ports World’s pur­chase of a port. It barred top-end chips from sale to China. With European gov­ern­ments, it stopped ASML, a Dutch maker of ma­chines cost­ing about $150 to 200 mil­lion each, from sell­ing to Chinese buy­ers. {#asml}
After Russia in­vaded Ukraine, about $600 bil­lion of its cen­tral bank’s re­serves held abroad were grabbed, and many Russian en­ti­ties were cut off from SWIFT. {#reserves}
## An au­di­ence of one

The moral case, Shah said, is that chok­ing an ag­gres­sor eco­nom­i­cally costs fewer lives than fight­ing with guns. And the re­sponse to Russia was meant for an au­di­ence of one, Xi Jinping: don’t you dare in­vade Taiwan. {017-C10}

Plenty of writ­ers have de­clared glob­al­i­sa­tion dead. Shah dis­agrees. Rogue states such as Russia, China, Iran and North Korea face the tool­kit. For Japan, Dubai or India, glob­al­i­sa­tion is great, and after COVID firms re­alised re­mote work­ers could just as well be in India.
~ Nor, he ar­gued, can any coali­tion of coun­tries build a cur­rency or pay­ment sys­tem to rival the dol­lar and the euro.

quote.text: And the trade-off your moral cal­cu­lus is be­tween the deaths of sol­diers and civil­ians ver­sus the ca­reer de­struc­tion for an AI re­searcher in China.

portraits.credit: Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain

sections.label: The babysitter
sections.head: In deficit, and delighted
sections.caption: trade deficits and babysitters
body: Amit Varma brought a third angle to the eco­nom­ics and geopol­i­tics: babysit­ters. In a 2005 *Financial Times* col­umn, Tim Harford noted that he pays his babysit­ter all the time and she buys noth­ing from him. {017-R18}
Treat them as coun­tries and you would see a trade deficit, Varma said. In fact they are two in­di­vid­u­als trans­act­ing to mu­tual ben­e­fit, just like Indians buy­ing from Chinese firms.

Ajay Shah called each deal a dou­ble thank-you mo­ment. The Indian im­porter tells his girl­friend he got a great deal; the Chinese ex­porter tells her boyfriend the same. “Everyone has a good ro­man­tic life in your sto­ries,” Varma ob­served. {017-J04}
## Count the hair­cut

Shah asked that goods and ser­vices be counted to­gether, since a wid­get, a potato and a hair­cut are all things you sell. That bal­ance equals the cur­rent ac­count deficit, which means cap­i­tal is com­ing in. He would wel­come cap­i­tal in­flows of 10 to 20 per cent of GDP a year. {017-C14}
Varma’s dis­quiet was for those out­side the club: the av­er­age Russian pa­triot, not fond of what Putin is doing, who still can­not get his McDonald’s burger. {#mcdonalds}
~ Pleased by Shah’s words, Varma still re­fused the bless­ing “aapke muh mein ghee shakkar”. Ghee is a su­per­food, he said; “avoid shakkar, it is poi­son.” {017-J05}

quote.text: It is in­di­vid­u­als, it is firms that do trade, not coun­tries that do trade.
And I will bor­row a piece of ad­vice from the great man Deng Xiaoping, which is bide your time. For 100 years, our jour­ney is to be­come an ad­vanced econ­omy and a democ­racy.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Butter, cigars, a soldier and a book: the tales the hosts couldn’t resist

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Polson, Amul and the taste of a bad train ride
stories.head: A butter too fresh for Bombay
body: During the First World War, the British Army wanted vast amounts of but­ter. Polson, a British com­pany that grew up in India, built the first milk sup­ply chain out of Gujarat, send­ing but­ter by train to Bombay and on to the UK. {#polson}
After the war Polson turned to the Indian mar­ket, and it dom­i­nated but­ter into the 1960s and early 70s. “As a child, I have eaten Polson but­ter,” Ajay Shah said.

Then came Amul. Kurien’s co­op­er­a­tive move­ment in Gujarat, with tech­ni­cal and fi­nan­cial sup­port, Shah be­lieved, from Denmark’s de­vel­op­ment aid agency, put new ma­chines and process de­signs into the milk sup­ply chain. Chilling plants and re­frig­er­ated vans car­ried clean, high-quality but­ter to Bombay.
Bombay hated it. The first batches flopped. Next to Polson, the city found Amul bland and dull: it did not have the punch of but­ter.

Investigators traced the cause to the rail­way. Refrigeration on the trains was poor, so Polson’s but­ter al­ways ar­rived from Gujarat a lit­tle ran­cid. “And the tastes of the Bombay con­sumer had be­come pro­grammed to ex­pect but­ter to taste a lit­tle ran­cid,” Shah said. {017-S01}

Amul had failed, in short, be­cause it was too good. So sci­en­tists worked out the exact chem­i­cals that form when but­ter goes ran­cid and added them to Amul’s. Shah did not know whether they per­sist to this day.
~ Amul took off in Bombay and drove Polson out of busi­ness. Amit Varma summed up the method: “They made it ran­cid de­lib­er­ately.”
stories.why: A wartime sup­ply chain shaped Bombay’s palate for half a cen­tury, and what the city called taste was a side ef­fect of bad re­frig­er­a­tion. A bet­ter prod­uct can lose until it re­pro­duces the flaws its cus­tomers have learned to ex­pect.
stories.postscript: Varma’s counter-story: Apple made its iPod shuf­fle less ran­dom so that it would feel ran­dom. {017-S03}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Polson’s rancid butter

stories.kicker: The story Amit Varma must tell, or his brain explodes
stories.head: A budget for Churchill’s ghost
body: In the 1980s, Amit Varma said, a de­part­ment of the Tamil Nadu gov­ern­ment called the CCA asked for a big­ger bud­get: its al­lo­ca­tion had been stag­nant for a long time. A cu­ri­ous bu­reau­crat went look­ing for its ori­gins.

They lay in the Second World War. Winston Churchill could not get his favourite Cuban cigars, and the world’s sec­ond-best cigars, Varma said, came from a town in Tamil Nadu. India was still British, so a de­part­ment was set up to sup­ply him: the Churchill Cigar Assistant.

Then, in Varma’s words, “World War II ended, Winston Churchill died, India gained in­de­pen­dence, not in that order.” {017-J06} The de­part­ment lived on into the 1980s, and “the per­son in it has the au­dac­ity to say we need more bud­get.” {017-S02}
~ Varma cred­its the story to a book by Bibek Debroy.
stories.why: A sup­ply chain born of a wartime short­age sur­vived its only cus­tomer for decades. Once a gov­ern­ment body ex­ists, it keeps jus­ti­fy­ing it­self long after any­one re­mem­bers why it was cre­ated.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Churchill’s Tamil Nadu cigars

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Walter Lippmann and a soldier left behind
stories.head: On guard for a finished war
body: Amit Varma read from the first chap­ter of Walter Lippmann’s *Public Opinion*. In 1914 a few Englishmen, Frenchmen and Germans lived on an is­land where the British mail steamer came only once in sixty days. {#sixtydays}
The war had bro­ken out, and for six weeks no­body there knew. “For six strange weeks they acted as if they were friends, when in fact they were en­e­mies,” Lippmann wrote. {017-C17}

It re­minded Varma of Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese sol­dier who landed on an is­land in the Philippines around 1944 with or­ders to de­fend it until death. “No one told him the war was over,” Varma said. For twenty-nine years he guarded it. {017-S04}
~ Varma first heard the story in Dan Carlin’s *Supernova in the East*. Lippmann’s chap­ter is called “The World Outside and the Pictures in Our Heads”.
stories.why: Lippmann’s point, as Varma used it: peo­ple act on the pic­tures in their heads, not on the world out­side. Without in­for­ma­tion, his ex­am­ples showed, a man can spend decades fight­ing a war that has al­ready ended.
stories.postscript: Varma said no tech­no­log­i­cal change has made Lippmann’s book, pub­lished at least a cen­tury ago, ob­so­lete.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Hiroo Onoda’s 29-year watch

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s pick: a book he could not put down
stories.head: Rush hour can wait
body: Ajay Shah was in Strand Book Stall in Bombay, with rea­son to hurry. He was due back in Bandra, and in rush hour, the sooner you left, the sooner you got home.
At ran­dom he came across David Kahn’s *Seizing the Enigma*. He read the first one or two pages, de­cided “this works”, and bought it. {017-R24}
Outside, those pages had left him trans­fixed. He wan­dered aim­lessly for a lit­tle while, then gave up, found a local Irani shop, sat down and read the whole book until 9 pm.
~ “The only one life I could imag­ine at that mo­ment was to drop ev­ery­thing and sit in an Irani shop and fin­ish the book,” he said. Amit Varma’s ver­dict: “This is the good life.” {017-S06}
stories.why: A great book can over­ride every plan for the day. Shah of­fered the tale as his rec­om­men­da­tion, a com­pan­ion to Varma’s weep­ing in the rain, and Varma saw it as the good life.

overheard.who: Amit Varma, after the hosts’ antakshari of stories

quiz.q: Why did Bombay first reject Amul’s butter, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: It was too good: Bombay was used to Polson’s slightly ran­cid but­ter.

quiz.q: What did the Tamil Nadu government department called the CCA originally do?
quiz.a: It sup­plied Tamil Nadu cigars to Winston Churchill dur­ing the Second World War.

quiz.q: Which five things crossing borders define globalisation in Ajay Shah’s account?
quiz.a: Ideas, peo­ple, goods, ser­vices and cap­i­tal, mov­ing through vol­un­tary trans­ac­tions.

quiz.q: In which year, by Shah’s account, did world trade-to-GDP regain its 1913 level?
quiz.a: 1982: free­dom was lost, Shah said, from 1913 to 1982 or be­yond.

quiz.q: What did Tim Harford’s babysitter show about trade deficits, as Amit Varma told it?
quiz.a: He pays her, she buys noth­ing from him, and both are bet­ter off.

quiz.q: Whose advice did Ajay Shah borrow for India in the third globalisation?
quiz.a: Deng Xiaoping’s: bide your time, and be­come an ad­vanced econ­omy first.

glossary.def: Using state power over the econ­omy to co­erce other coun­tries.
About 150: the re­la­tion­ships hu­mans are wired to sus­tain.
Why trade helps both, even when one side is bet­ter at ev­ery­thing.
A sta­tis­ti­cal check for ran­dom­ness that counts streaks of each length.
A chain game: each turn starts from the last syl­la­ble.
Ghee and sugar, from a bless­ing on someone’s wel­come words.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 17. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Winston Churchill (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Bruce Springsteen (Raph_PH, CC BY 4.0); William Edward Hartpole Lecky (Julia Margaret Cameron (1815-1879), public domain); Peter Singer (Ula Zarosa, CC BY 2.0); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); David Ricardo (Thomas Phillips, public domain); Xi Jinping (Presidencia de la República del Ecuador, public domain); Tim Harford (PopTech, CC BY-SA 2.0); Walter Lippmann (Pirie MacDonald, public domain); Robin Dunbar (Festival della Scienza from Genova, CC BY-SA 2.0).

shelf.title: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
shelf.creator: Robin Dunbar
shelf.why: Dunbar’s find­ing that we can sus­tain only about 150 mean­ing­ful re­la­tion­ships, in tiers of roughly 5, 15, 50 and 150, with most of our emo­tional en­ergy going to the clos­est few.

shelf.title: History of European Morals
shelf.creator: W.E.H. Lecky
shelf.why: The source of the ‘ex­pand­ing circle’: through his­tory we ex­tend moral con­sid­er­a­tion from fam­ily to tribe to na­tion and be­yond.

shelf.title: The Expanding Circle
shelf.creator: Peter Singer
shelf.why: Singer’s ar­gu­ment that our moral cir­cle keeps widen­ing and will one day in­clude an­i­mals.

shelf.title: An American Tail
shelf.creator: Don Bluth
shelf.why: He used it to mock the idea of a lost golden age of plenty in India’s past, and to argue that philoso­phies like Jainism arose de­spite scarcity, not be­cause of abun­dance.

shelf.title: Dawn of the third globalisation?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s ‘novel insight’ that glob­al­i­sa­tion isn’t dead: it now runs in­side a club of well-behaved coun­tries, en­forced through eco­nomic state­craft, and ex­cludes rogue play­ers.

shelf.title: An Indian view on dollar domination
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Expands on why anger at the power of the ad­vanced economies won’t pro­duce a work­able al­ter­na­tive, and why India should sim­ply play by the rules of the game.

shelf.title: Cross-border activities in India need more freedom, not less
shelf.creator: Pratik Datta and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Pratik Datta and Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that the Indian state’s fine-grained con­trol of cross-border cap­i­tal curbs the nat­u­ral free­doms of peo­ple and firms, and that its anti-internationalisation stance needs to go.

shelf.title: The importance of services exports
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Shows how tele­com made ser­vices trad­able and why re­mote work after COVID opened a new phase of glob­al­iza­tion for India.

shelf.title: When world leaders thought you shouldn’t need passports or visas
shelf.creator: Jo Adetunji
shelf.why: Documents how re­cent and avoid­able state con­trol of human move­ment re­ally is.

shelf.title: How Amul became utterly butterly delicious and salty
shelf.creator: Vikram Doctor
shelf.why: Tells the full his­tory of how Amul’s first, too-perfect but­ter flopped in Bombay be­fore it won the mar­ket.

shelf.title: Making it Less Random
shelf.creator: Lapham’s Quarterly
shelf.why: Covers how a prod­uct had to be en­gi­neered to match people’s faulty in­tu­itions about ran­dom­ness.

shelf.title: Unlikely is Inevitable
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s col­umn on the law of truly large num­bers: with a big enough sam­ple, un­likely runs are bound to hap­pen, so los­ing sev­eral hands in a row as an 80% favourite is nei­ther a rigged game nor proof of a bad de­ci­sion, and bad luck shouldn’t be read as fate.

shelf.title: Comparative Advantage explained
shelf.creator: Econlib
shelf.why: A clear ex­plainer of why trade ben­e­fits both sides even when one is bet­ter at ev­ery­thing.

shelf.title: The Great Redistribution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­ket in­ter­ven­tions such as tar­iffs or bans on FDI in re­tail qui­etly move money from many dis­persed, poor con­sumers to a few or­gan­ised, rich in­ter­est groups, the op­po­site of their stated in­ten­tion.

shelf.title: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Where the hosts first laid out how prices carry in­for­ma­tion and in­cen­tives that change the be­hav­iour of con­sumers and pro­duc­ers, and how tar­iffs re­dis­tribute wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: The China Model is Broken
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Chinese state con­trol and in­dus­trial pol­icy caused deep prob­lems be­hind the cherry-picked EV and solar suc­cesses: Xi’s cen­tral­i­sa­tion and na­tion­al­ism, cap­i­tal con­trols, real-estate over­build­ing, the exit of for­eign­ers and a failed eq­uity mar­ket.

shelf.title: ‘Stop the war.’ 44 Top Russian Players Publish Open Letter To Putin
shelf.creator: Sam Copeland
shelf.why: Amit sees these play­ers as the true pa­tri­ots: they stood up for their coun­try by op­pos­ing its state.

shelf.title: A trade deficit with a babysitter
shelf.creator: Tim Harford
shelf.why: Harford al­ways pays his babysit­ter and she buys noth­ing from him, yet both are bet­ter off: a neat de­mo­li­tion of panic about bi­lat­eral trade deficits and of the mis­lead­ing word ‘deficit’.

shelf.title: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s ac­count of re­vers­ing his di­a­betes through diet: eat less ce­real, avoid pro­cessed food, and treat ghee as a su­per­food and sugar as poi­son.

shelf.title: Public Opinion
shelf.creator: Walter Lippmann
shelf.why: Lippmann’s cen­tury-old mas­ter­piece on how the media shapes what we be­lieve and what to watch out for, which no tech­no­log­i­cal change has made ob­so­lete; Amit says ev­ery­one should read it.

shelf.title: Hardcore History
shelf.creator: Dan Carlin
shelf.why: One man reads around forty books per episode and then sim­ply talks, with no script, co-host or sound ef­fects, and it is riv­et­ing.

shelf.title: Supernova in the East
shelf.creator: Dan Carlin
shelf.why: It is the source of the story of the sol­dier who de­fended a Philippine is­land for 29 years be­cause no­body told him the war was over.

shelf.title: Blueprint for Armageddon
shelf.creator: Dan Carlin
shelf.why: The Hardcore History se­ries that kept Amit out­side his build­ing after runs, weep­ing in the rain: the let­ters sol­diers wrote to their wives and girl­friends the night be­fore a reck­less mis­sion in which they all died taught him the power of audio sto­ry­telling, along with lessons on re­silience, tragedy and the folly of na­tion states.

shelf.title: Seizing the Enigma
shelf.creator: David Kahn
shelf.why: Its first two pages gripped him so com­pletely that he skipped his com­mute and read the whole book in an Irani cafe until 9 pm.

laughs.text: Ajay ex­plains that Indian cap­i­tal con­trols let only poul­try farms and nan­otech­nol­ogy firms bor­row abroad. Amit: ‘So if you’re a re­ally small chicken, you have the best of both worlds, poul­try farms and nano chicken.’

Amit’s ver­sion of com­par­a­tive ad­van­tage: ‘I am a bet­ter pod­caster than you. I am also a bet­ter econ­o­mist than you. However, I do the pod­cast­ing and I let you do the eco­nom­ics be­cause hey, I can’t spend all my time doing eco­nom­ics.’

After Ajay ex­plains that ASML’s ma­chines make chip tracks about ten sil­i­con atoms wide, Amit asks what the sen­sual or­ganic sound is called when these atoms brush against each other: ‘ASMR by ASML.’

Ajay de­scribes an Indian im­porter telling his girl­friend he got a great deal on Chinese goods, while the Chinese ex­porter tells her boyfriend she got a great price from India. Amit: ‘Everyone has a good ro­man­tic life in your sto­ries.’

Pleased by Ajay’s words, Amit re­fuses to say the tra­di­tional bless­ing ‘aapke muh mein ghee shakkar’ be­cause he re­versed his di­a­betes (Episode 9). He keeps the ghee, ‘a superfood’, and drops the sugar: ‘Avoid shakkar, it is poi­son.’
Amit’s Churchill cigar time­line: ‘World War II ended, Winston Churchill died, India gained in­de­pen­dence, not in that order.’

Ajay on the op­ti­mism of the sec­ond glob­al­iza­tion, when the West wel­comed ev­ery­one un­con­di­tion­ally: ‘We felt con­fi­dent that as you be­come rich, you will in­evitably stop beat­ing your wife.’
Ajay on a worn-out word: ‘By the time a word grad­u­ates into the air­port books, you know, it surely stops mak­ing much sense.’
An American Tail: to de­bunk myths of a lost golden age, Ajay quotes the fable told to the mice in Russia: ‘there are no cats in America and the streets are filled with cheese.’

Chintaman Deshmukh took part in the Bretton Woods ne­go­ti­a­tions. Amit adds that Keynes wanted him as the IMF’s first man­ag­ing di­rec­tor, but the Americans ob­jected: ‘What Indian fel­low, what are you talk­ing about?’
Ajay on why Nazi Germany in­tro­duced the world’s first cap­i­tal con­trols: ‘Nazi is German for na­tion­al­ist so­cial­ist,’ and Hitler brought in the con­trols when he wanted to go after the Jews.

Amit com­pares fu­ture judge­ment of meat-eaters to how we view slav­ery: just as Jefferson kept slaves and thought it morally fine, peo­ple two hun­dred years from now may look back and say ‘oh they ate an­i­mals.’
Bibek Debroy, cred­ited by Amit as the source of the Churchill Cigar Assistant story.
